source.title: Sparse Crosscoders for diffing MoEs and Dense models
source.authors: Marmik Chaudhari; N. Hundia; I. Gulati

record.tranche_reason: Tests dictionary-based recovery of features in trained dense and MoE language models using crosscoders, rather than the original toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports crosscoder reconstruction, feature counts and densities, and decoder-cosine diagnostics. The λs/λf experiments and chosen ratio are method-tuning results, not rows. It does not test superposition geometry, neuron polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality.
record.test_reason: The paper uses BatchTopK crosscoders to compare a 5-layer dense model with a 5-layer MoE. It does not test whether real models hold sparse, recoverable features. The ~87% variance explained is the tool's reconstruction performance, with no sparsity level, control or interpretability check; the authors say feature meaning still needs validating. The feature counts and densities are outputs used to compare the two architectures, not evidence on superposition. This is T4: the finding is used as a tool, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that crosscoders can be applied to some extent to architectural diffing. They report ≈87% variance explained, fewer MoE-specific than dense-specific features, and denser MoE-only features but sparser Dense-only features relative to shared ones. They also say crosscoders need modification for structurally distinct models and that features need qualitative validation. The abstract further claims MoEs develop more specialized representations while dense models spread information across general features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses BatchTopK crosscoders to analyze learned features in independently trained Dense and MoE models; it does not use the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the previously suggested λs/λf ratio of 0.1–0.2 did not work well in this setting and that approximately 0.7 was needed; this was method tuning, not a claim-result row.

fits_no_version.finding: The MoE has far fewer model-specific crosscoder features than the dense model (910 vs 3,226). MoE-only features are denser than shared features; Dense-only features are sparser.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MoE architectures learn fewer, more specialized features than dense models with matched active parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: A standard crosscoder labels many features as shared despite near-zero decoder cosine. Non-budgeted shared-range features include cosine ≈ −1. The usual trimodal ∆norm distribution does not appear.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Crosscoder shared/exclusive classifications are unreliable when comparing independently trained, structurally different models.

record.problems: Only two trained models are compared; no uncertainty estimates or control models are reported. The authors state that qualitative analysis is still needed to validate the semantic meaningfulness and relevance of discovered features, and note limitations of crosscoders for structurally distinct models.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's λs/λf experiments and selected hyperparameter are omitted because they are method-tuning results rather than outcomes on the claim's subject.

untested.parts: No toy-model experiment, sparsity transition or geometry analysis.
No neuron polysemanticity or capacity competition is measured.
No measurement of polysemantic neurons or their alternative causes.
Does not test whether features are spread across neurons, or whether dictionary features are genuine. The crosscoder is used only as a diffing tool on two small 5-layer models.
No test of whether features are complete, stable or canonical, beyond the noted unreliability of shared-feature classification.

missing.what: No clear trimodal ∆norm distribution, unlike crosscoders used to diff base and fine-tuned models.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's verdict that this tests V4 (T2) is rejected. The paper uses crosscoders as an instrument and reports their performance and outputs on tiny models, with no validation of the features. Its findings concern MoE-versus-dense differences and crosscoder reliability, neither of which is a version of the claim. The λs/λf tuning is correctly left out as method tuning.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-model superposition experiment, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry is tested.
No neuron polysemanticity or competition for limited dimensions is measured.
No polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity are measured.

Tests crosscoder recovery in the paper's trained models, not feature distribution across neurons or recovery in large pretrained LLMs; semantic validity of the discovered features is not qualitatively assessed.
Does not establish whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional features with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Measured fractional variance explained by a BatchTopK crosscoder trained on third-layer outputs.
rows.measure: Fractional variance explained of model activations
rows.note: Reported as a crosscoder result for the paired models; the text does not give separate values for each model.
rows.check: ~87% FVE is the crosscoder's own reconstruction performance, not a measure of whether the models hold sparse recoverable features. No L0 or sparsity level, baseline or interpretability check is given. The subjects are tiny 5-layer models trained from scratch.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Counted features classified as MoE-only by relative decoder-norm difference.
rows.note: Feature count reported for the paired-model crosscoder.
rows.check: A count of MoE-only features is a dictionary output used for model diffing. It cannot show whether V4 holds.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Counted features classified as Dense-only by relative decoder-norm difference.
rows.note: Feature count reported for the paired-model crosscoder.
rows.check: A count of Dense-only features is a dictionary output used for model diffing. It cannot show whether V4 holds.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Counted features classified as shared by relative decoder-norm difference.
rows.note: Feature count reported for the paired-model crosscoder.
rows.check: The shared-feature count is a dictionary output. The paper itself says many shared classifications are unreliable (near-zero or −1 cosine).

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation densities of MoE-only features with shared features.
rows.value: MoE-only features have higher density than shared features
rows.note: No numerical density values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Comparing feature density across architectures is not a V4 measure.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Compared activation densities of Dense-only features with shared features.
rows.value: Dense-only features have lower density than shared features
rows.note: No numerical density values are stated in the text.
rows.check: Comparing feature density across architectures is not a V4 measure.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder-vector cosine similarity for features classified as shared by a standard crosscoder.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between model-specific decoder vectors
rows.value: Many features classified as shared had near-zero cosine similarity
rows.note: The authors interpret this as the standard objective overestimating shared structure when model activations differ substantially.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Compared decoder-vector cosine similarity for explicitly budgeted shared features.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between model-specific decoder vectors
rows.note: The paper distinguishes these explicitly budgeted features from other features falling in the shared ∆norm range.

rows.subject: Dense and MoE models
rows.operation_detail: Examined decoder-vector cosine similarity for other features in the shared ∆norm range.

conditions.value: shared ∆norm range 0.3–0.7, excluding budgeted shared features

rows.measure: Cosine similarity between model-specific decoder vectors
rows.value: Not consistently high; some features had cosine similarity ≈ −1
rows.note: The text reports a range of outcomes within this feature group.
